title_en: Chinese man earns US$7,500 a month running mobile eyelash studio from car
content_en:
Xiaofei became a full-time eyelash technician 3 years ago, following previous jobs as a bus mechanic, electric welder, and truck driver.
A Chinese business owner has found success in the mobile beauty industry, earning 50,000 yuan (US$7,500) per month by offering eyelash extensions from his car. Photo: SCMP composite/Douyin
A man from southwestern China has attracted online attention after claiming to run a “profitable” mobile eyelash studio from his car.
Xiaofei, a man in his 30s from Chongqing municipality, said on his short-video account that his eyelash extension business brings in a guaranteed monthly income of 50,000 yuan (US$7,500).
Already the owner of an eyelash extension shop in the city, Xiaofei recently expanded his business by offering mobile services to clients.
He set up a studio in his car and drives to meet customers, bringing the service virtually to their doorsteps.
Xiaofei said the mobile studio has allowed him to expand his business beyond the district where his shop is based and serve clients across the city.
Xiaofei shared that the mobile studio lets him reach clients across the entire city, taking his business well beyond his shop’s home district. Photo: hntv.tv
He came up with the idea after noticing that customers wanted him to offer services in their homes.
However, as nearly all his customers are women, Xiaofei found it inconvenient to work inside their homes. He came up with the idea of serving them in his car instead.
He covers the front seat with a disposable sheet, takes a “before” photo of each customer, then uses photo-editing software to try out different eyelash styles. He projects the images onto the car’s screen so customers can choose their preferred look.
A session usually takes about an hour, which is considered quick in the industry. Xiaofei said his speed comes from his experience and skill.
Some customers even fall asleep during the service.
He charges 300 to 500 yuan (US$45 to US$75) per customer, depending on the service and style – prices that are higher than the market average.
Xiaofei drapes a disposable sheet over the front seat to turn his car into a mobile salon, snaps a “before” photo, and digitally tests different eyelash styles on the client. Photo: hntv.tv
Xiaofei became a full-time eyelash technician three years ago. Before that, he worked as a bus mechanic, an electric welder and a truck driver.
Before taking on those jobs, which are traditionally considered more “manly,” Xiaofei had studied permanent make-up. He also met his wife eight years ago while learning make-up application.
When they planned to marry, his future father-in-law opposed their working in the beauty business, believing it would not provide a steady income and could lead to a break-up.
Xiaofei put his family first and took steady jobs that provided social insurance.
He spent all his savings on their wedding to create lasting memories. In turn, his wife invested her entire dowry in his start-up, which ultimately failed.
Three years ago, after getting his father-in-law’s approval, Xiaofei trained in eyelash extensions and opened his business.
Delivering professional service as one of the region’s first specialists in Chinese-style lash extensions, Xiaofei has built a large base of regular clients. Photo: hntv.tv
He said he was among the first in the region to specialise in Chinese-style eyelash extensions, attracting many regular customers to his shop.
He has also expressed gratitude in his videos for his wife’s unwavering support.
Xiaofei’s videos drew many comments praising the mobile studio as a smart idea.
“This is a smart way to offer eyelash extension services in a car. It’s cost-effective, convenient and safe,” one commenter wrote.
“There’s no one right answer when it comes to a profession. As long as someone is skilled and understands what their customers want, a car can serve as a fully functioning studio,” another commented.
By Fran Lu

title_en: Thomas Markle charged in US with possessing child sex abuse material
content_en:
Grand jury indictment in Los Angeles raises federal counts to two after Philippines probe and Florida arrest.
Thomas Markle in custody after he cut off an electronic ankle monitor he was ordered to wear. Photo: Pinellas County Sheriff’s Office via Reuters
Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain’s Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, and father-in-law of Britain’s Prince Harry, was indicted on Tuesday in US federal court on two counts of ‌possessing child sexual abuse material.
The indictment doubles the number of federal charges currently lodged in Los Angeles against the 82-year-old Markle in a case that grew out of an investigation initiated last month in the Philippines, where he previously resided.
The elder Markle was originally charged on November 5 in a criminal complaint with a single felony count of possessing child sexual abuse images.
According to an FBI affidavit filed with the complaint, the material in question was found in ⁠two Los Angeles storage units and included two explicit photos of Markle posed with a naked underage girl and other images ‌of him with children in various stages of undress.
One of the photos showed a naked girl in a room that appeared to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines, the affidavit ‌said.
Philippine police said last week criminal complaints had been filed against Markle in the country’s Cebu province, where he ⁠once lived, accusing him ⁠of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children.
Thomas Markle in court in Tampa, Florida. Illustration: Douglas A. Land via AP
Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the claims were untrue and describing ‌them as “sick lies”.
He was arrested on November 6 at a Florida assisted-living facility where he has been a patient, and is expected to be transferred to California ‌in the ‌coming weeks to be arraigned in US District Court in Los Angeles on the two-count grand jury indictment returned on ‌Tuesday.
Following a court-ordered psychiatric evaluation of Markle, a US magistrate judge in Tampa, Florida, last week ruled that he was mentally ⁠competent to stand trial, meaning that he understood the proceedings against him and could assist in his own defence.
Each count of possession ⁠of child sexual abuse material, an offence referred to in the US criminal code as possession of child pornography, is punishable by up to 20 years in prison if he is convicted, the US attorney’s statement ‌said.
Meghan Markle, an American actor, has ‌been estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage to King Charles’ younger son, Harry, in 2018, when the duchess has said she first became aware of allegations against her father.
She has said she was “deeply distressed” over the matter, which led her to cut off contact between her father and her two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5.
By Reuters

title_en: China enlists builders of world’s highest bridge to repair runways in wartime
content_en:
Analysts say peacetime training ensures skilled civilian crews are ready to fill critical gaps if conflict breaks out.
A key challenge is adapting civilian construction practices to wartime requirements, when speed becomes critical. Photo: Xinhua
China is enlisting civilian engineers who helped to build the world’s highest bridge to repair airfields in wartime as part of wider efforts to integrate civilian expertise into its defence preparations.
The Chinese military’s PLA Daily reported on Monday that authorities in Guiyang, southwestern China’s Guizhou province, had formed a specialist militia company comprising road and bridge workers from an unnamed major firm involved in building the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge. The 2.9km (1.8 mile) bridge rises 625 metres (2,050 feet) above the bottom of a gorge.
Analysts say the Chinese authorities are setting up dedicated units in peacetime to ensure that civilian resources are organised, trained and available before the start of a potential conflict, rather than relying solely on emergency requisitioning once hostilities break out.
While China’s use of civilian resources for defence is not new, a 2025 study by the US-based National Bureau of Asian Research found that the country’s mobilisation system had placed greater emphasis on wartime preparations since 2015.
A ceremony in January last year marks the completion of the main structure of the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge in southwest China’s Guizhou province. Photo: Xinhua
These preparations span sectors ranging from construction to rail and commercial shipping. Under China’s National Defence Mobilisation Law, revised in August, organisations in key sectors must set up and train specialist support teams in peacetime.
Those efforts are also very important for the PLA Air Force.
A 2023 report by the US Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI) noted that, following the 1991 Gulf war, the People’s Liberation Army concluded that its airfields would likely come under attack early in a conflict with the United States.
The institute assessed that quickly resuming air operations could complicate US efforts to establish air superiority and divert American resources from other operations.
The bridge stands 625 metres above a gorge in Guizhou. Photo: Xinhua
Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said the survival and repair of airfields was “critical in a battle for air superiority”.
He said damage to runways not only prevented aircraft from carrying out their missions but also left them stranded on the ground as “mass targets for follow-on air or missile strikes”.
“If there are no hardened aircraft shelters, it can be like shooting fish in a barrel,” he said.
While the PLA has its own specialist airfield repair units, it also draws on civilian engineers and equipment.
Bosack said engineering units that could respond rapidly tended to be limited in number but in high demand, adding that having designated civilian personnel provided “backup options that can fill critical gaps”.
[embedded media]
According to the PLA Daily report, existing militia repair units in Guiyang’s Nanming district could not handle extensive runway damage or major disruptions to road networks.
To address that shortfall, local authorities began recruiting skilled workers from the transport infrastructure sector in 2022, drawing on the expertise of the construction firm, which has built 28 bridges ranked among the world’s 100 highest.
A key challenge is adapting civilian construction practices to wartime requirements, when speed becomes critical.
The militia company has since repeatedly trained alongside active-duty troops, practising runway surveys, rubble clearance and emergency concrete pouring, with military units setting repair deadlines and standards.
The construction firm stores the heavy machinery and materials, while military and civilian authorities jointly manage them for peacetime and wartime use.
Timothy Heath, founder of US-based consultancy Perceptum and a specialist on the Chinese military, said organising and training civilian personnel in peacetime should make wartime mobilisation “more efficient and less chaotic”.
“War is inherently chaotic,” Heath said, adding that peacetime preparations and training could improve the performance of government and military personnel under wartime pressures.
The Guizhou initiative is not an isolated case. Similar militia units were established and trained for airfield repairs in Shandong province in 2018, Jiangsu province in 2024 and in April this year in Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan province neighbouring Guizhou.
[embedded media]
The CASI study found that agreements with civilian organisations specified responsibilities and, in some cases, emergency response times. Civilian support for military airfields extended beyond runway repairs to medical assistance, air traffic control and fuel supplies.
The PLA is also exploring ways to accelerate airfield recovery using uncrewed systems. In October, state-run Science and Technology Daily reported that a naval aviation unit under the Southern Theatre Command had conducted a joint military-civilian exercise simulating the aftermath of an air strike.
Drones mapped runway damage while robotic dogs used lasers to deal with unexploded ordnance and uncrewed ground vehicles removed hazardous explosives before repair crews moved in.
Beijing has also explored using civilian airports and highways as alternatives when damaged runways cannot be repaired quickly.
While China has been conducting highway landing exercises since 1989, a 2024 article in the PLA Daily noted that few highways could withstand the impact of modern fighter jet landings.
“Once a runway is damaged, warplanes cannot take off or land and supplies cannot get through. Every additional minute of delay increases the risk,” the PLA Daily quoted an exercise controller as saying during a drill review.
[embedded media]
Heath said repair times would depend on the severity of the damage, “but with the right training and materials, runways could be repaired within hours”, while Bosack said recovery speed also depended on “the nature of the damage and the needs of the aircraft”.
Yet peacetime drills may not fully reflect wartime conditions. The CASI study noted that some exercises began with workers and equipment already on site, rather than testing how quickly they could be mobilised.
Heath also warned that civilian experts could be harmed in the fighting and that “skilled personnel could then become in short supply”.
Despite these challenges, Bosack said the main value of having civilian personnel available to supplement military engineering units lay in sustaining operations beyond 30 days.
“They won’t provide much use in a fast-moving crisis or contingency, but they certainly could in a full-blown conflict,” he said.
By Gabriel Dominguez

title_en: China’s Shenzhou-24 spacecraft lifts off with first foreign astronaut on board
content_en:
The country’s latest mission includes Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who will spend around a week on the Tiangong space station.
A Long March-2F Y24 rocket carrying the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft blasts off to China’s Tiangong space station from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in Gansu province on Wednesday. Photo: Reuters
China’s latest crewed space mission, Shenzhou-24, lifted off on Wednesday morning, taking three astronauts – including the first foreign crew member – to the Tiangong space station.
In a sign of the space programme’s increasing diversity, for about a week, the station will be home to four astronauts from mainland China, one from Hong Kong and one from Pakistan.
A Long March-2F rocket carrying the spacecraft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in the northwestern province of Gansu at 8.18am, according to the China Manned Space Agency.
The astronauts in the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft on their way to the Tiangong space station. Photo: CCTV
Bathed in an orange sunrise, the rocket rose from the launchpad with a deafening roar, sending massive plumes of smoke and desert dust into the sky.
Mission control declared the launch a success 22 minutes after lift-off. Once in orbit, Shenzhou-24 will travel to the Tiangong and dock in 3½ hours – all going to plan.
The crew of three consists of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, as well as payload expert Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, Pakistan’s first astronaut in orbit.
“I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut, one flight to multiple joint flights, the moon, Mars and beyond,” Ali said on Tuesday.
[embedded media]
Ali will stay in the Tiangong for about a week and will return to Earth on Shenzhou-23 together with Zhang Zhiyuan and Hong Kong’s first astronaut Lai Ka-ying, who have spent the past six months on the space station.
Tang and Wu will spend six months on the Tiangong together with Zhu Yangzhu, the third member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, who will become the first Chinese astronaut to spend a whole year in space.
Zhu’s experiences will be used to study how the human body adapts to long periods in space and to test health, work and living support systems for astronauts, Zhang Jingbo, a spokesman for the China Manned Space Agency, said.
The data collected will help support future missions.
Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali (left) and Chinese astronauts Wu Yi (centre) and Tang Hongbo attend a send-off ceremony at the launch centre on Wednesday. Photo: Xinhua
Beijing plans to send three astronauts to the moon before 2030, two of whom are expected to set foot on the lunar surface.
During the Shenzhou-24 mission, the crew will carry out 90 experiments and test technology used in fields such as space life sciences, aerospace medicine, microgravity fluid physics and combustion.
The mission will include four joint China-Pakistan projects in biotechnology and materials science.
Ali will be the first foreign astronaut to board the space station. During his time in space, he will carry out experiments on photosynthesis in bacteria and the impact of space radiation and microgravity on quinoa seeds, according to Cang Huaixing, a researcher at the Technology and Engineering Centre for Space Utilisation at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
[embedded media]
Chinese is the main working language on the space station. Ali had no knowledge of the language when he was selected for the mission but after seven months of training, he said he would be able to communicate with the other astronauts in Chinese.
Wu Dawei, from the China Astronaut Research and Training Centre, said the training team had compiled glossaries of space flight terms and procedure checklists with audio recordings to help Ali practise.
He had also learned some Chinese songs to help him understand the language.
“For this short-term rotation mission, he has met the basic Chinese-language requirements, and our astronauts have also undergone relevant English training. When necessary, we [the astronauts] will use both Chinese and English to ensure they clearly understand the mission status and respond properly,” Wu added.
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali pictured during a training session. Photo: Xinhua
Ali would also have a halal menu during his stay aboard the Tiangong, tailored to both his nutritional needs and personal preferences, she said.
China has been trying to diversify its crewed space programme in recent years. Lai from the Shenzhou-23 crew was Hong Kong’s first astronaut and a candidate from Macau is also undergoing training.
[embedded media]
By Ji Siqi

title_en: South Korea’s Lee clears out ‘self-reliance’ camp ahead of Trump G20 summit
content_en:
President Lee Jae Myung’s latest nominations bolster his pro-alliance camp as Seoul seeks to unlock stalled security talks with Washington.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung speaks during a meeting with senior presidential secretaries at Cheong Wa Dae in Seoul in November 5. Photo: EPA / Yonhap
South Korea’s reshuffling of its top diplomatic and security officials could help repair strained ties with Washington and, in turn, ease complications in Seoul’s relationships with Beijing and Pyongyang, analysts said.
President Lee Jae Myung on Monday moved to replace his foreign minister, unification minister and intelligence chief – a shake-up that removes two prominent advocates of greater diplomatic autonomy from Washington and inter-Korean reconciliation.
While the changes suggest a shift towards a more alliance-centred approach, observers said they were more likely to reflect a tactical adjustment than a wholesale reversal of Lee’s foreign policy.
The overhaul comes as negotiations with Washington over key security issues – including South Korea’s acquisition of nuclear-powered submarines, the transfer of wartime operational control and the revision of a bilateral nuclear cooperation agreement – have made little headway.
Outgoing National Intelligence Service (NIS) director Lee Jong-seok and Unification Minister Chung Dong-young were regarded as leading figures in the administration’s jaju (self-reliance) faction, which favours greater strategic autonomy and a more balanced approach towards China and the United States.
Their counterparts in the dongmaeng (alliance) faction, led by National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac, place greater emphasis on Seoul’s alliance with Washington. Wi has retained his post.
Observers said the reshuffle also signalled President Lee’s desire to mend fences with Washington ahead of next month’s Group of 20 summit in Miami, where Seoul is reportedly exploring a meeting with US President Donald Trump – potentially over a round of golf.
US President Donald Trump shakes hands with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on Thursday. Photo: AP
“This reshuffle could be seen as a victory by the [pro-US] alliance faction over the self-reliance faction,” Kim Joon-hyung, parliamentary floor leader of the splinter opposition Rebuilding Korea Party, said. “This is apparently designed to appease Washington, but it remains to be seen how well it will go down with Washington.”
Washington reportedly harboured reservations about Chung and Lee Jong-seok’s foreign policy positions, particularly their push to maintain a balance between China and the US.
Bilateral intelligence cooperation also deteriorated during Lee Jong-seok’s tenure as NIS chief. Earlier this year, Chung publicly disclosed an unconfirmed North Korean uranium enrichment site in Kusong, reportedly prompting Washington to restrict the sharing of sensitive intelligence with Seoul – compounding friction as President Lee clashed with Washington over Seoul’s regulatory crackdown on US-listed e-commerce company Coupang following a massive customer data breach.
Under Monday’s nominations, Wi’s deputy, second deputy national security adviser Lim Woong-soon, has been nominated as the new foreign minister. Outgoing Foreign Minister Cho Hyun is reportedly among the candidates being considered for South Korea’s ambassador to Washington.
Former justice minister and judge Kang Kum-sil has been nominated to replace Lee Jong-seok as NIS chief, putting her on track to become the first woman to head the agency since its establishment in 1961.
Meanwhile, Hong Ihk-pyo, a former Democratic Party lawmaker who recently served as Lee’s senior political affairs secretary, has been nominated as the new unification minister.
The appointments are expected to consolidate Wi’s influence as national security adviser, potentially tilting policymaking towards a more alliance-centred approach, observers said.
South Korean National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac speaks during a press briefing at Cheong Wa Dae in Seoul in November. Photo: EPA / Yonhap
“This cabinet reshuffle is interpreted as a step towards restoring relations with the United States and strengthening the foundations of the South Korea-US alliance,” said Kim Jae-chun, an international relations professor at Sogang University. “The appointments suggest an intention to repair ties with Washington by replacing officials regarded as advocates of greater diplomatic autonomy.”
Cho, who was himself seen as an advocate of strengthening the US alliance, was also replaced – apparently to minimise potential backlash from the government’s traditional support base over the removal of more autonomy-minded officials, Kim added.
The nomination of Lim, who is considered close to Wi, as foreign minister also pointed to continuity in the administration’s broader diplomatic direction, he said.
As for Hong, Professor Kim described the unification minister nominee as a moderate pragmatist with expertise in diplomacy, security and inter-Korean affairs. Unlike Chung, who drew criticism from conservatives for advocating sanctions relief to facilitate dialogue with Pyongyang, Hong was unlikely to make controversial public statements that could complicate ties with Washington, Kim said.
Presidential Chief of Staff Lim Kwang-hyun dismissed concerns that the sweeping changes signalled a shift in the administration’s foreign or North Korea policies, saying the move was meant to “inject vitality into the government administration and accelerate the implementation of state affairs”.
“With the international order in flux, we will seek to achieve maximum results through pragmatic diplomacy and take the lead in opening the path to peaceful coexistence on the Korean peninsula, while firmly protecting the people’s safety and welfare,” he told reporters on Monday.
Choi Jin, director of the Institute of Presidential Leadership, said friction with the Trump administration over Seoul’s earlier autonomy-driven approach had stalled both bilateral cooperation and efforts to revive inter-Korean and US-North Korean dialogue.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks with outgoing South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun at the State Department in Washington in February. Photo: Getty Images via AFP
“The reshuffle can therefore be understood as a response to the difficulties the government’s dialogue-oriented policy and efforts to address outstanding issues had encountered because of US reservations about some of the previous officials,” Choi said.
“The underlying view is that difficulties in South Korea-US relations tend to spill over into Seoul’s relations with both Beijing and Pyongyang,” he said, adding that the shake-up was intended to inject fresh momentum into those diplomatic initiatives without abandoning overall policy continuity.
“The new appointees are not considered particularly hostile towards China. They are also seen as being receptive to a policy of diplomatic balance between the United States and China and are therefore expected to pursue such an approach,” Choi said.
Not all observers viewed the shake-up as a net positive. Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies, warned that the Korean peninsula remained unstable despite Seoul’s outreach to China and Russia alongside its US alliance.
“At a time when we need active diplomatic efforts to manage the situation, these changes risk creating a vacuum in diplomacy,” he said.
The centre-left Hankyoreh daily echoed that caution in an editorial on Tuesday, pointing to the unresolved North Korean nuclear issue and growing concerns over sphere-of-influence politics among major powers.
“It is imperative to pursue an independent and multifaceted foreign policy that does not rely solely on the United States,” it said.
By Park Chan-kyong

title_en: As CATL’s grip on Chinese EV makers loosens, Xpeng doubles down on battery production
content_en:
New battery lines seek to boost supply chain flexibility as Chinese carmakers diversify suppliers and pressure CATL’s dominance.
Xpeng vehicles roll off a production line. Photo: Handout
Chinese electric vehicle (EV) maker Xpeng is ramping up its battery pack manufacturing despite widening losses, seeking greater supply chain independence as carmakers continue to diversify away from Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL).
The Guangzhou-based firm recently signed a 1.8 billion yuan (US$270 million) agreement with Zhaoqing municipal government in southern China’s Guangdong province to establish an integrated automotive project, according to a social media post by the local government on Monday.
The project would include new battery pack production lines with an annual capacity of about 200,000 units, alongside new vehicle models and a global after-sales spare parts supply chain centre.
A battery pack is the complete energy-storage system installed in an EV, consisting of battery cells, a management system, thermal management technology and other hardware.
Often regarded as the heart of an EV, it typically accounted for about one-third of a vehicle’s total cost, according to a 2021 report sponsored by Swiss-Swedish industrial technology giant ABB.
While cost savings from bringing battery pack assembly in-house would be relatively limited, carmakers were increasingly looking to reduce reliance on any single supplier’s control at the pack level, said Lucas Zhang Liutong, director of Hong Kong-based consultancy WaterRock Energy Economics.
“In-house packing is a low-hanging fruit,” Zhang said. “It can make [battery] cells more interchangeable and strengthen the automaker’s negotiating position when facing battery leaders like CATL and BYD.”
Chinese carmakers, including Xiaomi and Li Auto, continue to diversify their battery supply chains amid deteriorating profitability and weakening domestic EV demand.
Xpeng, CATL’s third-largest client in 2021, had already switched most of its battery sourcing to CALB Group and EVE Energy in recent years, with only its Mona model using batteries supplied by BYD, according to a company source.
The latest investment comes as Xpeng’s net loss widened 129 per cent year on year to 870 million yuan in the third quarter.
With carmakers diversifying suppliers, CATL’s share of China’s EV battery market declined for six consecutive months, falling to 40 per cent in October, although it remained the market leader, according to data from the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance.
Second-tier battery makers were rapidly gaining ground while smaller players were accelerating their exit from the market, creating a more fiercely competitive industry landscape, said Cui Dongshu, secretary general of the China Passenger Car Association, in an analysis released on Monday.
At the same time, CATL and other Chinese battery makers faced growing overcapacity risks as energy-storage installations in China fell short of expectations and potential US import restrictions clouded demand prospects, analysts said.
By Themis Qi

title_en: US soldier Jian Zhao admits selling military information to Chinese buyers
content_en:
The US Army sergeant took photos of restricted documents and also offered to sell computers and hard drives.
The US Department of Justice said that Jian Zhao conspired with a former US Army soldier to obtain and transfer information and equipment related to the national defence to buyers in China. Photo illustration: AP
An American soldier who sold what he claimed was top secret know-how to Chinese-linked buyers faces up to a decade in prison after admitting passing on sensitive military information.
Army sergeant Jian Zhao, 37, took advantage of his security clearance to get his hands on restricted documents.
He snapped pictures of military information on his mobile phone and offered to sell military computers and government hard drives, as well as details about communications networks, rocket and missile systems and military exercises.
“By his own admission, Jian Zhao – a member of the US Armed Forces – betrayed the country he swore an oath to defend by providing the Chinese government with sensitive US military information,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.
The US Department of Justice said for more than three years, Zhao conspired with Ruoyu Duan, a former US Army soldier, to obtain and transfer information and equipment related to the national defence to buyers in China.
A screenshot shows a US Justice Department press release on Jian Zhao’s case. Image: US Justice Department
Duan, who previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defence information, recruited active-duty US military personnel, including Zhao, to provide defence-related information and facilitated communications and financial transactions with China-based buyers.
Zhao was arrested at his home in Washington state in March 2025, where agents found US$30,000 in cash as well as electronic devices and multiple Army hard drives.
Zhao faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison, a US$250,000 fine and up to three years of supervised release.
He is scheduled to be sentenced on March 1, 2027.

title_en: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang says he is in therapy, as comeback rally fades
content_en:
Huang says he made ‘some terrible mistakes’ at an hour-long all-hands meeting a day after being reinstated as CEO.
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang attends the US-Saudi Investment Forum in Washington in November 2025. Photo: Reuters
Jensen Huang apologised to Nvidia staff and said he was in therapy on Tuesday, as a stock rally triggered by his shock return as CEO faltered amid persistent doubts over the probes he faces and the fate of the AI investment boom.
“I made some terrible mistakes,” Huang told an hour-long all-hands meeting at the company’s Santa Clara, California, headquarters, The New York Times reported after reviewing a live stream of the event.
He told staff it was “not acceptable” that he had broken a code of conduct he had helped write, and dismissed suggestions that he was back because US President Donald Trump had pressured the board.
But Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been in contact with directors about Huang’s return. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump said. “And I convinced them.”
After vaulting more than 30 per cent on Monday, Nvidia shares were down about 6 per cent at close on Tuesday.
[embedded media]
“The optimism faded quickly” for Nvidia, wrote Fawad Razaqzada of Forex.com, with “questions over corporate governance and board oversight still lingering”.
So far Monday’s surge was a “one day wonder … We are not seeing an upside follow through today at all,” said Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of Mahoney Asset Management.
Huang resigned on November 12 over extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, a departure that sent shares in Nvidia and companies closely linked to the AI buildout tumbling.
Trump was reportedly talked into backing the return of the Taiwan-born CEO after top tech investors told him the US economy and Wall Street depended on it.
Nvidia said on Monday that it had reinstated Huang as chief executive after receiving information from the US government that he did not pose a national security risk.
Trump is also an investor in Nvidia, owning as many as 370,000 shares in the company as of September 30, according to filings.
Nvidia trades are displayed on a ticker at the New York Stock Exchange on Monday. Photo: Reuters
Shares linked to the AI boom have fallen steeply in recent weeks amid fears that the AI bubble, inflated since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, was finally bursting.
In downward-trending markets, quick rebounds are common but “tend to get negated and that has been the sequence since early October,” Mahoney said, adding that “sellers have absolute control of the market here”.
Nvidia is central to the AI investment story – its powerful processors are the key tool to train and run the AI models that are believed to be at the heart of a technological revolution.
The massive spending on its AI chips and software, housed in sprawling data centres, catapulted the company into the ranks of the world’s most valuable firms.
Huang used that success to turn Nvidia into a kind of central bank for other AI companies and start-ups, doling out loans and financial guarantees to firms that would otherwise struggle to borrow from traditional lenders.
Investors are also weighing a barrage of legal challenges facing Huang and Nvidia.
[embedded media]
The board that let Huang go and then rehired him is still overseeing an internal investigation into concerns that he may have been the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, even though Trump says he has been cleared.
The Justice Department is separately investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that allegedly bought Nvidia processors and routed them to Chinese customers in violation of US export restrictions.
The Securities and Exchange Commission has also reportedly opened a probe into Nvidia’s accounting practices and potentially misleading communication to shareholders.
“Nvidia is a good corporate citizen. That shouldn’t be groundbreaking,” US Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters at an unrelated press conference in Washington on Tuesday.
“If Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn’t be the message that the president is saying to the American people,” he added.
Huang will nevertheless face lawmakers at a closed-door hearing before three House committees on December 1 and a live-streamed Senate committee hearing on December 3.
Lawmakers from both parties have expressed anger over the circumstances of Huang’s return, and the scrutiny is likely to intensify in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.

title_en: Why Asia’s AI rally faces a tougher road even after Jensen Huang’s comeback
content_en:
Chip and AI investment growth is unlikely to match first-half highs as US scrutiny of the sector intensifies, analysts say.
Jensen Huang's return follows a turbulent fortnight for Asia’s tech-heavy markets. Photo: EPA
While Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia has soothed market sentiment, analysts have warned that the artificial intelligence boom that propelled Asian chip stocks this year is unlikely to regain its first-half momentum – and that US regulatory scrutiny of the sector remains far from over.
“The market is certainly, at least for a day, soothed by the fact that Jensen is back,” said Brian Levitt, chief global market strategist at investment management firm Invesco, at a media briefing on Tuesday.
Nvidia shares jumped more than 31 per cent after the board reinstated the company’s co-founder as CEO on Monday. The S&P 500 climbed 4.7 per cent, halting a seven-day run of declines, and the Nasdaq 100 surged nearly 7 per cent.
His return follows a turbulent fortnight for Asia’s tech-heavy markets. The MSCI Asia-Pacific index endured an eight-day losing streak and slid towards bear-market territory, while Taiwan’s benchmark Taiex plunged 17.5 per cent the previous week.
Even with Huang back at the helm, Levitt cautioned that the explosive growth in AI infrastructure investment and chip-sector earnings seen earlier this year was unlikely to return.
“I don’t think we’re ever going back to the rate of investment or the rate of earnings growth that we saw in the first half of the year,” Levitt said. “Those were the fireworks.”
Levitt said investors had worried because Huang had become one of the biggest backers of investment across the AI industry, earning Nvidia the nickname “the Bank of Jensen”. Because the company continued to generate significant cash flow, many of those investments were likely to continue, he added.
Nvidia and the AI industry have their core figure back, but Asia’s old normal has not returnedNatixis analysts
Still, a slower pace of AI capital expenditure would be less favourable for chipmakers and memory-chip producers, while benefiting large cloud providers – or hyperscalers – that already controlled computing capacity and held ample cash reserves, Levitt said.
He urged investors in Asia to watch their exposure to semiconductor and memory-related trades, noting that emerging-market outperformance this year had been “very much driven by a handful of stocks”, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and SK Hynix.
Huang resigned on November 12 following reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman whom US officials suspect of spying for China – an allegation Beijing has denied.
The episode has fuelled bipartisan calls in Washington for tougher curbs on China’s access to advanced chips, given Nvidia’s central role in powering cutting-edge AI models and its importance in the broader US-China tech rivalry.
[embedded media]
Analysts at investment bank Natixis, including chief Asia-Pacific economist Alicia Garcia-Herrero, wrote on Tuesday that while the risk of Nvidia “sailing without a captain” had passed, “the script for the AI growth story has changed”.
They warned that investors should not assume US restrictions on the sector had reached their peak.
A US rule that took effect on Thursday restricts large-scale Chinese access to advanced chips through overseas data centres and generally requires licences for covered chip exports from US companies, including Nvidia, to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil.
In response to compliance and security concerns, Nvidia reportedly set up a board committee focused on national security and export controls on November 17 and is searching for a chief compliance officer.
Huang is also due to answer questions from US House committees in private on December 1 and from the Senate Banking Committee in public on December 3, ahead of Democrats taking control of Congress in January.
“What has not changed is that a growing US-China rivalry [continues to have consequences] and how security outranks commerce whatever [US President Donald] Trump agrees with [President] Xi [Jinping],” the Natixis analysts said.
“Nvidia and the AI industry have their core figure back, but Asia’s old normal has not returned.”

title_en: Brazil’s ‘Lithium Valley’ makes its play for BYD as three states fight over new EV plant
content_en:
Incoming state government wants the Chinese carmaker to build a full supply chain from lithium ore to batteries.
BYD employees work on the production line at the company’s plant in Camacari, Brazil. The Chinese electric carmaker will build a new factory in Brazil to produce electric buses, trucks and vans. Photo: Reuters
Chinese carmaker BYD said on Tuesday it will sign a memorandum of understanding with Brazil’s Minas Gerais state in January as it weighs where to build a factory for electric buses, trucks and vans that Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro are also trying to attract.
BYD’s Brazil vice-president Alexandre Baldy confirmed plans to sign the agreement after January 6, when Cleitinho Azevedo, the governor-elect of Minas Gerais, takes office.
Cleitinho met BYD executives in Sao Paulo and was upbeat about the talks.
“They are making this commitment that from January 6, there will be a lot of investment in Minas Gerais,” he said.
Vice-governor-elect Luis Eduardo Falcao said the state wants more from BYD than an assembly line.
[embedded media]
“Our strategy to attract investment to Minas Gerais will prioritise the energy transition. More than a possible car factory, we are working for BYD to be a major partner in developing the whole chain, from ore to batteries and electric vehicles,” he said.
Last December BYD told the South China Morning Post it planned to build the new plant in Sao Paulo state, where it already assembles electric bus chassis in the city of Campinas. But plans seem to have changed since then.
Minas Gerais is Brazil’s second-most populous state and the country’s main mining region, and it is also home to a large car industry built around the Stellantis plant in Betim.
The Jequitinhonha Valley in the state’s northeast holds about 85 per cent of Brazil’s lithium reserves, and the local government has been promoting it to investors as the “Lithium Valley”. The mineral is a key input for the batteries that BYD makes for its own vehicles.
The plant is expected to cost about 1 billion reais (about US$169 million) and employ around 2,000 people when production starts between 2028 and 2029.
Neither the state nor BYD has disclosed what tax incentives are on the table. Minas Gerais usually offers investors deferred state VAT on imported machinery and tax credits on sales, but the state owes the federal government about 180 billion reais (US$30.4 billion) and is on a 30-year debt repayment plan.
Brazil’s tax reform will start phasing out the state VAT in 2029, which would reduce the long-term cost of such breaks.
Cleitinho wants the factory in the Jequitinhonha Valley, where BYD already buys lithium from Brazilian Lithium Co. and other miners.
But Falcao said the company would make the final decision, depending on logistics. Mining companies in the valley complain of frequent power failures and bad roads, and the area is one of the poorest in Brazil.
BYD needs more capacity in Brazil because demand for its electric buses has outgrown the Campinas operation.
The site built about 600 chassis from 2015 to 2025 while bus operators were slow to switch to electric models. Orders picked up after the pandemic as cities replaced old fleets, and BYD expects to build around 1,200 chassis in 2026.
BYD’s director for commercial vehicles Marcelo Schneider told SCMP that the company is already running out of space for new orders and that the new plant could make 6,000 to 7,000 chassis a year.
He said BYD would use Brazil to supply electric buses to other South American countries and could later export to Africa.
By Igor Patrick

title_en: Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts after months-long battle in US courtroom
content_en:
Chinese tech giant found guilty of bank and wire fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and evading sanctions.
Huawei faced 12 criminal counts in the US, including racketeering conspiracy, bank fraud and trade secret theft. Photo: Reuters
The nearly seven-year US criminal case against Huawei Technologies and three subsidiaries finally ended on Tuesday when a jury in Brooklyn found that the company was guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including bank and wire fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and evading sanctions.
But the jury found the technology company not guilty of conspiracy to obstruct justice or conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act, or Rico, the most serious and potentially consequential charge, which the company framed as a partial win.
“It’s premature to comment on what the sentence would be,” said lead defence lawyer Brian Heberlig. “There are very serious penalties associated with Rico, potential forfeiture of parts of the enterprise, which the government alleged in this case was Rico. That’s all out the window.”
The exhaustive legal case, filed by the US Justice Department in January 2019, has involved dozens of lawyers, hundreds of motions and filings, millions of documents and tens of millions in legal fees.
Huawei faces huge potential penalties, including massive financial fines and regulatory restrictions. Motions and responses in advance of sentencing are scheduled to start in the third week of January.
[embedded media]
Heberlig said Huawei was considering its options, including moving for a new trial based on disputed evidentiary rulings or an appeal.
The jury, which has been on the case since September 8, also found Shenzhen-based Huawei and its subsidiaries guilty of violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and money laundering.
Jurors began deliberations on the afternoon of November 18, meaning the panel spent five days weighing evidence.
Judged by its length, scope, geopolitical implications and breadth of evidence, this was among the most complex corporate trials in history. Pre-trial manoeuvring alone lasted seven years and nine months, while testimony lasted some 10 weeks.
Overseen by US District Judge Ann Donnelly, the demands of sifting through millions of pages of technical source code, banking records, foreign emails, closed-courtroom testimony and sensitive witnesses required numerous protective orders not usually seen outside espionage or terrorism trials.
“Rarely has a jury had to commit so much of their personal time to a trial,” Donnelly said in dismissing the jury. “I thank you for your service.”
Prosecutors during the trial argued that Huawei operated a conspiracy dating back to the 1990s that employed corporate espionage, fraud and stolen secrets as a central strategy to expand globally.
They further argued that the company deliberately deceived HSBC and other global clearing banks to present its Iran subsidiary, Skycom Tech, as an independent entity not subject to US financial sanctions.
To bolster its case, prosecutors called more than 60 witnesses who alleged that Huawei stole router source code from Cisco Systems, cellular transmission designs from Motorola, networking equipment information from Fujitsu and robotic testing equipment from T-Mobile.
“Huawei cultivated a culture of crime and corruption, and that crime was an important business strategy,” US prosecutor Taylor Stout said in an opening statement in September.
Huawei called some 15 witnesses in countering that it flourished through its own innovation, research and development (R&D) and relentless home-grown engineering that generated numerous patents at the hands of a now 110,000-person R&D operation.
The company relied for its defence on a team of lawyers from Sidley Austin, Steptoe and Jenner & Block.
“Huawei’s success did not come from theft, racketeering or fraud. It came from the same hard work that guided Mr Ren,” Heberlig said. “It’s about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”
Heberlig further argued that prosecutors “began with guilt and worked backwards”, singling out isolated compliance shortcomings from decades of global business.
The verdict came days after US President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
“We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit,” Huawei said in a statement. “We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”
The huge privately held multinational company, a Chinese national champion, was started by founder Ren Zhengfei in his Shenzhen flat in 1987 with the equivalent of US$5,000. In 2025, Huawei reported revenue of CNY880.9 billion (US$126 billion) from operations in over 170 countries.
The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But China’s foreign ministry has repeatedly condemned the US prosecution as politically motivated “lawfare” and economic coercion.
“The Chinese government firmly opposes the US side’s suppression and containment of Chinese enterprises,” said ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun in September. “China firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests.”
In the lead-up to the case, Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou was arrested in 2018 for bank and wire fraud. She pleaded not guilty to criminal charges and paid no fine, but admitted to misleading HSBC, which may have influenced Tuesday’s jury decision.
[embedded media]
“A factor, but one of many,” said Heberlig. “But who knows? I can’t really get into their heads.”
In a case involving eye-glazing testimony centred on accounting, corporate manuals, immigration documents and flow charts, a centrepiece of the government’s case was an internal video taken by T-Mobile.
At the time, Huawei was having quality control problems with its handsets and testing equipment, and T-Mobile had developed a robot it nicknamed “Tappy” that could test devices at high speed.
The video allegedly shows a Huawei engineer identified in filings as “A.X.” unbolting and detaching Tappy’s robotic arm assembly, sliding it into his backpack and walking out. When T-Mobile discovered it missing, the engineer claimed it fell into his bag by “mistake” and that he returned it the next day. Huawei subsequently fired him.
In a related incident, the government cited as evidence a visiting engineer from China, Wang Yu, who was escorted into a restricted lab where he allegedly measured Tappy’s components and worked with “A.X.” to assess the robotic arm overnight before it was returned.
“Today’s verdict makes clear that fraud, sanctions evasion and the theft of intellectual property are not business strategies,” said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle in a statement. “They are serious crimes. Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft.”
Huawei argued such allegations were extremely rare and the work of a rogue employee rather than a feature of its corporate culture, citing its extensive safeguards and compliance. The tech giant added that employee incentives were in line with industry standards and not aimed at rewarding trade-secret theft.
Responding to the banking and sanction evasion charges, Huawei argued that senior management in no way sought to mislead global financial institutions.
Furthermore, it said, sophisticated global players like HSBC have extensive compliance, monitoring and experience with Skycom’s operations and knowingly processed transactions driven by the profits these generated.
It is unclear what impact the verdict will have on Huawei’s business. US authorities had argued for years that Huawei posed national security risks and blocked it from key US markets. But the firm has shifted gears, moving into artificial intelligence and expanding into non-US markets.
Heberlig noted the long road that the case has travelled – many companies settle in similar situations – adding that Huawei never wavered in its commitment to defend itself in court.
“There was a pandemic in the middle that came and went,” he said. “There were four superseding indictments by the end of the day. Some counts were dismissed voluntarily by the prosecution before trial.
“It was a very complex sort of roller coaster ride.”
By Mark Magnier

In the lead-up to the case, Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou was arrested in 2018 for bank and wire fraud. She pleaded not guilty to criminal charges and paid no fine, but admitted to misleading HSBC, which may have influenced Tuesday’s jury decision.
[embedded media]
“A factor, but one of many,” said Heberlig. “But who knows? I can’t really get into their heads.”
In a case involving eye-glazing testimony centred on accounting, corporate manuals, immigration documents and flow charts, a centrepiece of the government’s case was an internal video taken by T-Mobile.
At the time, Huawei was having quality control problems with its handsets and testing equipment, and T-Mobile had developed a robot it nicknamed “Tappy” that could test devices at high speed.
The video allegedly shows a Huawei engineer identified in filings as “A.X.” unbolting and detaching Tappy’s robotic arm assembly, sliding it into his backpack and walking out. When T-Mobile discovered it missing, the engineer claimed it fell into his bag by “mistake” and that he returned it the next day. Huawei subsequently fired him.
In a related incident, the government cited as evidence a visiting engineer from China, Wang Yu, who was escorted into a restricted lab where he allegedly measured Tappy’s components and worked with “A.X.” to assess the robotic arm overnight before it was returned.
“Today’s verdict makes clear that fraud, sanctions evasion and the theft of intellectual property are not business strategies,” said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James Barnacle in a statement. “They are serious crimes. Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft.”
Huawei argued such allegations were extremely rare and the work of a rogue employee rather than a feature of its corporate culture, citing its extensive safeguards and compliance. The tech giant added that employee incentives were in line with industry standards and not aimed at rewarding trade-secret theft.
Responding to the banking and sanction evasion charges, Huawei argued that senior management in no way sought to mislead global financial institutions.
Furthermore, it said, sophisticated global players like HSBC have extensive compliance, monitoring and experience with Skycom’s operations and knowingly processed transactions driven by the profits these generated.
It is unclear what impact the verdict will have on Huawei’s business. US authorities had argued for years that Huawei posed national security risks and blocked it from key US markets. But the firm has shifted gears, moving into artificial intelligence and expanding into non-US markets.
Heberlig noted the long road that the case has travelled – many companies settle in similar situations – adding that Huawei never wavered in its commitment to defend itself in court.
“There was a pandemic in the middle that came and went,” he said. “There were four superseding indictments by the end of the day. Some counts were dismissed voluntarily by the prosecution before trial.
“It was a very complex sort of roller coaster ride.”

title_en: Trump awards Rudy Giuliani the Medal of Freedom, highest US civilian honour
content_en:
The former New York mayor became hugely popular in American politics after the 9/11 attacks and has been a staunch ally of the US president.
Donald Trump (right) and Rudy Giuliani pose for photographs at the Trump National Golf Club Bedminster clubhouse in New Jersey in  November 2016. Photo: AP
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday awarded the Medal of Freedom, the country’s highest civilian honour, to Rudy Giuliani, the former New York mayor who became a national figure after the September 11, 2001, attacks and later helped Trump try to overturn his 2020 election defeat.
Trump announced he would honour Giuliani, 82, ‌in September 2025 shortly after the former mayor was badly injured in a car accident. Trump at the time called him “the greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot”.
After the September 11 attacks, Giuliani became one of the most popular figures in US politics. He launched a Republican presidential bid in 2007, and even after it failed, he remained a prominent conservative messenger.
In a statement, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales called Giuliani “a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New ⁠York City and our nation”.
Trump awarded the medal in a private Oval Office ceremony.
Andrew Giuliani speaks with reporters as his daughter tries to pull him away at the White House on Tuesday. Photo: AP
Giuliani in a statement said he was “honoured and humbled” ‌by the medal, and credited advice from President Ronald Reagan, under whom he served as associate attorney general and a US Attorney, for guiding his public service.
“I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with ‌me, disagreed with me, and loved me – particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together,” Giuliani ⁠said.
His son, former Trump administration ⁠official Andrew Giuliani, told reporters outside the White House that the ceremony was a “special” gathering in which Trump and Giuliani reminisced about their long friendship.
Their alliance deepened after Trump lost ‌the 2020 election. Giuliani advanced falsehoods about the result and the integrity of the voting process.
He held a press conference at a Philadelphia landscaping business, where he made claims that were widely ‌rebutted, then ‌another at the headquarters of the Republican National Committee where hair dye dribbled down his face.
His false claims came with legal consequences.
He ‌was barred from practising law in New York, where he once served as the US Attorney in the state’s southern district, and Washington, and faced criminal ⁠charges in Georgia and Arizona for attempting to subvert the 2020 election results.
[embedded media]
Two Georgia election workers won a US$148 million judgment against Giuliani in December ⁠2023 for defamation. He “fully satisfied” the terms of the judgment in February 2025.
By the end of that year, Trump pardoned him for federal criminal offences.
With Giuliani’s medal, Trump has awarded the Medal of Freedom 27 times between his two terms.
He has ‌predominantly reserved the honour – designated by President ‌John F. Kennedy for “meritorious contribution” to US security or national interests, world peace or cultural endeavours – for former athletes.
Fourteen of Trump’s awards have been to retired athletes, some of whom also served in public office.
He has said he plans to award the medal to retired and scandal-plagued Major League Baseball pitcher Roger Clemens and US national hockey team goaltender Connor Hellebuyck.
Trump posthumously awarded the medal to slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk in October 2025.

title_en: Gisele Pelicot slams publisher for using nude images from her rape case in book promo
content_en:
Intimate photos of her taken by her rapist ex-husband were used as promotional material for a book about her fight for justice.
Gisele Pelicot leaves after attending a ceremony marking the laying of the foundation stone for the Women’s House in Nice, France, on Monday. Photo: AFP
Gisele Pelicot says she is deeply shocked that a Paris publishing house used nude images taken of her by her rapist ex-husband as promotional materials for a book that examines her watershed fight for justice.
The 73-year-old Pelicot became an icon of courage and feminist causes during the drugging-and-rape trial in 2024 that convicted all 51 of the accused men, including her ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot.
In a statement to BFMTV, Gisele Pelicot denounced the book, Emprises, and the publisher’s use of intimate photos in promoting it. The broadcaster published extracts of the statement on Monday.
“I am deeply shocked that images of the most private aspects of my life could be exhibited and exploited for commercial gain,” the statement said, according to BFMTV. “I refuse to let my private life be used as a selling point.”
The nude images of Pelicot were apparently taken by Dominique Pelicot and were part of the court case that saw him sentenced to 20 years in prison, said Christophe Bigot, a lawyer for Gisele Pelicot.
A protester holds a placard reading “If it’s not a ‘yes’, then it’s a ‘no’” during a demonstration in support of Gisele Pelicot in Rennes, France, in September 2024. Photo: AFP
Bigot said he had seen the images and that they show Gisele Pelicot alone, without the men convicted for rapes and sexual assaults while she was unconscious, knocked out with drugs that Dominique Pelicot slipped into her food and drink.
Gisele Pelicot’s statement also criticised the book itself, saying it “describes scenes of me being raped and gives an interpretation of my life that is unbearable”.
“Above all, I refuse to let my story be rewritten to suggest that I was complicit with what I was subjected to,” she said, according to the statement extracts.
“Today, I find myself humiliated, exposed and hurt once again. As if the ordeal of the trial hadn’t been enough!”
The publisher, Editions Tinbad, did not respond on Tuesday to emailed questions. On its website, Tinbad acknowledged that promotional efforts had been “unfortunate and ill-suited”. It offered “our sincerest apologies” to Pelicot and to author Sabine Prokhoris.
It said that it would not print any additional runs of the book beyond the 280 copies now in the hands of its distributor, and that it would stop promoting it.
But it said that “absolutely no images of her being raped or video of a pornographic nature were sent to the press”.
Gisele Pelicot speaks after she receives Freedom From Fear Medal in Middelburg, the Netherlands, in April. Photo: AP
The weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaine first reported last week that the publisher sent photos and videos of Gisele Pelicot to several media outlets. The newspaper described the images as pornographic and said they were taken by Dominique Pelicot.
It quoted Tinbad’s publisher as saying: “Of course we don’t have Mrs Pelicot’s permission to distribute these photos. That is why we sent them to you solely for private, informational purposes.”
The police evidence against Dominique Pelicot included his library of images documenting years of abuse – more than 20,000 photos and videos in all, stored on computer drives and catalogued in folders marked “abuse”, “her rapists”, “night alone” and other titles.
He and all but one of his co-defendants were convicted of sexually assaulting Gisele Pelicot over a period of nearly a decade. The other co-defendant was convicted of drugging and raping his own wife with Dominique Pelicot’s help.
Gisele Pelicot became a hero to many in France and beyond for courageously demanding that all the evidence be heard in open court, waiving her right to anonymity as a survivor of sexual abuse and insisting that shame should fall on her abusers, not her.
By Associated Press

title_en: Jensen Huang’s return steadies Nvidia, but China curbs, US scrutiny show no sign of easing
content_en:
US congressional investigations and export-control concerns continue to weigh on Nvidia’s business in China and Southeast Asia.
Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Photo: Reuters
Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO may steady the chipmaker’s leadership and calm jitters across the global artificial intelligence supply chain, but it is unlikely to ease US export restrictions on China as national security scrutiny in Washington intensifies, analysts say.
The reinstatement of Huang on Monday, ending an 11-day leadership crisis at one of the world’s most valuable companies, sent Nvidia shares surging more than 31 per cent to close at US$165.05 on the Nasdaq, adding nearly US$1 trillion in market value.
At Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California, employees greeted his return with cheers and applause, the South China Morning Post reported.
While the move was expected to help restore confidence across the global AI computing supply chain and reinforce prospects for AI infrastructure buildouts, it did not “signal a substantial change in US restrictions on exports of advanced computing chips to China”, Guotai Haitong Securities said in a research note on Tuesday.
A reprieve for Huang, the brokerage noted, did not translate into greater room for Nvidia to sell its products in China. Nvidia confirmed during its earnings call last week that it had halted shipments of US-licensed Hopper chips, including the H200, to the country.
Analysts warned against interpreting the leadership reversal as a softening of Washington’s tech containment strategy.
“Congressional momentum towards tighter restrictions is still moving ahead,” said Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow on the Chinese economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s (ASPI) Centre for China Analysis.
Dan Ives, an analyst at US merchant bank Yorkville Ives, echoed that assessment in a note to clients on Monday, writing that Huang’s return had done little to clear the regulatory cloud hanging over the company.
Both Nvidia’s internal investigation and government inquiries remained active, he said, while “the export question has not been resolved”.
White House intervention
The dramatic turnaround caps a tumultuous period that began on November 12, when Huang resigned after admitting to marital infidelity, following reports linking him to Alice Huang, a businesswoman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has repeatedly dismissed the espionage allegation.
His departure sparked a lobbying campaign by employees, investors and Silicon Valley figures, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, calling for his return. Although Huang signalled his willingness to come back at the height of the push, Nvidia’s board initially resisted before reversing course on Monday.
In a statement, the board said it voted unanimously to reinstate Huang following input from US government officials, concluding that his return “poses no national security risk”.
We don’t believe that Nvidia is back to even with the start of the sagaMorningstar
Nvidia also said days earlier that it had established a national security and export control committee, made up entirely of independent directors, to oversee trade-compliance matters.
Behind the scenes, US President Donald Trump played a decisive role, reportedly dialling into an Nvidia board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return, according to US news outlet Semafor. Trump later told American broadcaster CNBC he had spoken with board members directly and indirectly to convince them to reverse course.
ASPI’s Lee said the White House’s intervention “mattered enormously” and underscored how central Nvidia and its founder had become to Washington’s AI ambitions, though she cautioned that the episode could invite even closer scrutiny of Nvidia’s ties to the Trump administration.
Pushback on Capitol Hill
Resistance on Capitol Hill showed no signs of fading. Republican leaders of three key House panels, including the House Select Committee on China, confirmed that Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter remained scheduled to appear for congressional interviews in early December.
“The Nvidia board’s brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed,” the lawmakers said in a joint statement on Monday.
They reiterated their commitment to investigating the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips and their role in advancing China’s AI capabilities.
[embedded media]
Beyond direct sales to China, the fallout threatened to complicate the broader global AI buildout, according to investment research firm Morningstar. While Huang’s return was likely to reduce the risk of disruptions to Nvidia’s product road map, Morningstar warned that a return to business as usual was far from assured.
Last week, the US Bureau of Industry and Security issued new rules requiring licences for advanced chips sent to overseas data centres that remotely supply large-scale computing power to Chinese and other restricted entities, closing what Washington viewed as a major loophole.
“We don’t believe that Nvidia is back to even with the start of the saga,” Morningstar said. “The company will face restrictions in selling leading artificial intelligence gear to countries, mostly in Southeast Asia, that were renting cloud workloads to Chinese AI model builders.”
By Ben Jiang, Ann Cao, Howard Liu

title_en: Huawei’s home-grown HarmonyOS passes 100 million device mark in ‘landmark moment’
content_en:
Tech giant plans to challenge Android and iOS internationally by gradually rolling out the operating system to global markets.
The logo of Huawei during the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on July 6, 2023. Photo: AFP
Huawei Technologies has announced that HarmonyOS, its home-grown, Android-free operating system, has surpassed 100 million installations, marking a milestone in its effort to build a software ecosystem independent of Google’s mobile services amid US-led sanctions.
The Shenzhen-based firm said the total was reached this month across smartphones, tablets and personal computers running HarmonyOS 5, 6 and 7. Its ecosystem now offered more than 460,000 apps and services from over 12 million registered developers, according to a Huawei statement on Tuesday.
In a social media post on Tuesday, Richard Yu Chengdong, chairman of Huawei’s Consumer Business Group, called the achievement a “landmark moment” and said the ecosystem had crossed a “critical scale threshold”.
“It has officially entered a new phase of maturity, usability and innovation-driven growth,” Yu wrote on China’s social media platform Weibo, which is similar to X.
The milestone comes two years after Huawei debuted HarmonyOS 5 in 2024, its fully self-developed operating system designed to replace Android on the company’s devices. Adoption quickly grew alongside the Chinese tech giant’s strong comeback in the smartphone industry, powered by in-house semiconductors, as the US-sanctioned company stepped up efforts to achieve self-reliance in software and hardware.
In China, HarmonyOS was the second-largest smartphone operating system in the second quarter, accounting for 24 per cent of the market, ahead of the 18 per cent by Apple’s iOS, according to data by Counterpoint Research. Google’s Android still led the market with a 58 per cent share.
Globally, HarmonyOS had only a 5 per cent share in the second quarter, compared with Android’s 75 per cent share and iOS’s 20 per cent, as limited app compatibility continued to limit its reach.
Huawei planned to make a stronger push to expand HarmonyOS internationally, “gradually” bringing the operating system to the global market in the next one to three years, Yu told reporters in September.
Huawei first launched HarmonyOS in China in August 2019, months after Washington added the company to a trade blacklist that blocked access to products using US-origin technologies without explicit approval.
Early similarities in HarmonyOS’s kernel – the core of an operating system that manages how software interfaces with hardware – initially made it compatible with Android apps. But that started to change with HarmonyOS 5, also marketed as HarmonyOS Next.

Huawei Technologies has announced that HarmonyOS, its home-grown, Android-free operating system, has surpassed 100 million installations, marking a milestone in its effort to build a software ecosystem independent of Google’s mobile services amid US-led sanctions.
The Shenzhen-based firm said the total was reached this month across smartphones, tablets and personal computers running HarmonyOS 5, 6 and 7. Its ecosystem now offered more than 460,000 apps and services from over 12 million registered developers, according to a Huawei statement on Tuesday.
In a social media post on Tuesday, Richard Yu Chengdong, chairman of Huawei’s Consumer Business Group, called the achievement a “landmark moment” and said the ecosystem had crossed a “critical scale threshold”.
“It has officially entered a new phase of maturity, usability and innovation-driven growth,” Yu wrote on China’s social media platform Weibo, which is similar to X.
The milestone comes two years after Huawei debuted HarmonyOS 5 in 2024, its fully self-developed operating system designed to replace Android on the company’s devices. Adoption quickly grew alongside the Chinese tech giant’s strong comeback in the smartphone industry, powered by in-house semiconductors, as the US-sanctioned company stepped up efforts to achieve self-reliance in software and hardware.
In China, HarmonyOS was the second-largest smartphone operating system in the second quarter, accounting for 24 per cent of the market, ahead of the 18 per cent by Apple’s iOS, according to data by Counterpoint Research. Google’s Android still led the market with a 58 per cent share.
Globally, HarmonyOS had only a 5 per cent share in the second quarter, compared with Android’s 75 per cent share and iOS’s 20 per cent, as limited app compatibility continued to limit its reach.
Huawei planned to make a stronger push to expand HarmonyOS internationally, “gradually” bringing the operating system to the global market in the next one to three years, Yu told reporters in September.
Huawei first launched HarmonyOS in China in August 2019, months after Washington added the company to a trade blacklist that blocked access to products using US-origin technologies without explicit approval.
Early similarities in HarmonyOS’s kernel – the core of an operating system that manages how software interfaces with hardware – initially made it compatible with Android apps. But that started to change with HarmonyOS 5, also marketed as HarmonyOS Next.

title_en: Hong Kong arts funding overhaul must help troupes thrive, not just survive
content_en:
While rising costs and lagging performance metrics make reform necessary, the changes must be shaped with the sector to protect artistic diversity.
A Hong Kong Ballet performance at Regent Hong Kong on September 21. Photo: Jonathan Wong
Hong Kong’s performing arts groups may not stand out as the world’s best. They have nonetheless built a strong following over the years and continue to enrich the city’s cultural landscape, thanks to government funding and commercial sponsorships. It is important that they continue to thrive and deliver quality work in a healthy environment.
A funding overhaul that links subsidies more closely to performance under the city’s first five-year plan and the chief executive’s policy address is meant to enhance standards in this respect. Under the new mechanism, the annual allocation for the existing nine major performing groups will comprise a “baseline subvention” and a “performance-based subvention”. The baseline component will gradually fall from about 77 per cent of the total to 50 per cent.
The performance-based component will take into account each group’s non-government revenue, including box-office takings, other operating income, donations and sponsorship, as well as its achievement of key performance indicators. Groups that perform well may receive more funding; those that persistently underperform may see their support reduced or, ultimately, lose major-group status. Conversely, a new “funding ladder” will be in place to enable smaller groups with good performance to eventually gain recognition as a major arts group for more funding.
The revamp is, in principle, a step in the right direction. At a time of fiscal pressure and rising expectations for accountability, public money should not flow automatically and indefinitely to organisations simply because they have long been designated as “major” groups. According to the government, the funding for the nine major groups has risen from about HK$220 million in 2007 to about HK$450 million (US$57.3 million) today, while paid attendance has fallen from 360,000 to 310,000 and the overall attendance rate has declined from about 77 per cent to 69 per cent during the period.
Those figures do not, by themselves, prove that the groups have failed. But officials say the gaps suggest that the value of public resources and the social value generated under the current funding mechanism have not yet been fully maximised. A serious review is therefore warranted.
Regardless of the benchmarks for assessment, the spirit of the reform should be to encourage arts groups to succeed through more targeted funding rather than punishing those that fail to meet the key performance indicators. Arts funding serves to enrich our cultural offerings, broaden public access and sustain groups and performances that may not always be commercially viable. A scheme that merely punishes poor performance via funding cuts would betray that purpose.
Whether the ultimate 50:50 ratio is the right split is a matter that should be seriously discussed with the sector. There are concerns about a vicious cycle where underperforming arts groups receive less funding to sustain certain programmes, which may in turn further affect overall performance. Exactly when and how a group will be stripped of its “major” group status is something to be worked out between the authorities and the arts sector after thorough consultation.
The KPIs will rightly take into account both quantitative and qualitative performance for a more holistic assessment. For instance, apart from quantitative measures such as the number of paid audience members, the number of paid performances and box office income, qualitative indicators will cover areas such as artistic excellence, talent grooming, audience building, community arts education, sound governance and management, and effective financial management and sustainability.
Hong Kong’s ambition to be an East-meets-West cultural hub under the five-year plan requires a sound arts ecosystem. That means a healthy mix of mainstream productions with broad public appeal and fringe and innovative work that caters for minority tastes and expands artistic boundaries. A well-balanced funding approach can stimulate creativity and enhance accountability while providing opportunities for promising lower-tier groups to step up and thrive. The onus is on the authorities and stakeholders to put in place the right funding mechanism so that the art scene can continue to flourish.
